rule: Target size proportional to importance and inversely proportional to distance from cursor. Important actions = large + close.
how_to_apply: Make primary CTAs the largest clickable element in their section. Place them near the content that motivates the click.
violation_example: Tiny 'Buy Now' button tucked in a corner far from the pricing info

rule: Decision time increases logarithmically with number of choices. Limit options per view to 5-7.
how_to_apply: Navigation: max 7 top-level items. Pricing: max 3-4 tiers. Feature grids: group into categories rather than flat lists.
violation_example: Navigation with 15 ungrouped links causing choice paralysis

rule: Working memory holds 7±2 items. Chunk information into digestible groups.
how_to_apply: Break long lists into groups of 3-5. Use visual separators between groups. Limit card grids to 3-4 per row.
violation_example: Speaker lineup showing 12 headshots in a single unbroken grid

rule: Users spend most time on OTHER sites. They expect yours to work the same way.
how_to_apply: Use conventional patterns: logo top-left links to home. Nav at top. Search with magnifying glass icon. Cart top-right.
violation_example: Custom hamburger menu on desktop where users expect horizontal nav

rule: Items close together are perceived as related. Items far apart are perceived as separate.
how_to_apply: Use tighter spacing within groups (8-12px) and wider spacing between groups (24-48px). Related form fields closer together.
violation_example: Equal spacing everywhere — user can't tell which label belongs to which input

rule: Items that look alike are perceived as having the same function. Same role = same visual treatment.
how_to_apply: All CTAs same style. All info cards same structure. Don't make one card in a grid look different unless it IS different.
violation_example: Three pricing cards where the recommended one uses completely different typography and layout

rule: The item that differs from the rest is most memorable. Use isolation for the ONE thing you want users to remember.
how_to_apply: Highlight the primary CTA with a different color. Make the recommended pricing tier visually distinct. Use a single accent color sparingly.
violation_example: Every element competing for attention with different colors and animations — nothing stands out

rule: Users judge an experience by its peak moment and its ending — not the average. Nail the hero and the final CTA.
how_to_apply: Invest most design effort in the hero section (first impression) and the closing CTA section (lasting impression). Middle sections can be simpler.
violation_example: Beautiful hero but the page trails off into a generic footer with no closing statement

rule: Incomplete tasks occupy the mind more than completed ones. Show progress to maintain engagement.
how_to_apply: Use progress indicators in multi-step flows. Show completion percentage. Partially reveal content to motivate scrolling.
violation_example: Multi-step form with no indication of how many steps remain or how far along the user is

rule: System response under 400ms feels instant. Anything slower needs visual feedback.
how_to_apply: Add loading states for any action taking >400ms. Use skeleton screens not spinners. Optimistic UI updates for common actions.
violation_example: Button click with no feedback for 2 seconds while API call completes — user clicks again
